1.pericope_label: The law resumed after the sentence in the wilderness

schools.summary: Gill fixes the moment. This comes after the murmuring over the spies' report, after the sentence that the generation should be consumed in the wilderness, and after the defeat at Hormah, and is spoken lest their posterity should be discouraged and despair of ever enjoying the good land. Calvin explains both what the accessory offerings are and why they are measured. In these oblations God consulted the rude condition of the people and took, as it were, the character of a man, as if he feasted familiarly with them, which is why he elsewhere calls the sacrifices his meat — not because he who is the life in himself and inspires the life of all requires the supports of life, but because unless he descends to men he cannot lift up their minds to things above. As to the measures, Moses partly adverts here to precepts handled more fully in Leviticus and partly gathers into one place what he had said in various places and more obscurely; but the real reason is the danger on the other side, lest the people should introduce many inane and superfluous pomps, as the Gentiles were foolishly and immoderately luxurious in their sacred feasts, as if their delicacies gave pleasure to God. The measure of each particular thing is therefore prescribed, that they may not dare to invent anything arbitrarily; for though the ceremonies might be of trifling importance in themselves, the lawful had to be carefully distinguished from the unauthorized, to forestall the licentiousness of men, who would otherwise not have failed to mingle their own leaven.

Henry hears in the law's opening words an answer to the sentence just passed. When you come into the land of your habitation which I give unto you is a plain intimation not only that God was reconciled to them notwithstanding what he had decreed, but that he would secure the promised land to their seed notwithstanding their proneness to rebel; the statute takes it for granted that some of them should in due time come into Canaan. On the offerings themselves he reasons domestically: since the sacrifices of acknowledgment were meant as the food of God's table, there had to be a constant provision of bread and oil and wine whatever the flesh-meat was, for it was fit that God should keep a good house, that his table should be furnished with bread as well as flesh, and that his cup should run over. From the tables of quantities he draws the plain moral, that our religious services should be governed, as by other rules, so by the rule of proportion.

Keil measures the silence the chapter interrupts. After the attempt to force an entry into Canaan against the will of God and the advice of Moses, the Israelites remained many days in Kadesh, then turned into the wilderness toward the Red Sea as they had been commanded, and did not come again to the desert of Zin until the first month of the fortieth year. All that is known of that interval is a list of encampment names, and since the situation of most of them is unknown, or at any rate undetermined, no connected account of Israel's movements through those thirty-seven years can be given.

outliers.note: marks the thirty-seven-year gap the chapter sits inside, and states plainly that the itinerary is too obscure to reconstruct — the narrative simply cannot be followed through this stretch

themes: a law that presupposes the land
God feasting with his people
the measure that forestalls invention

2.pericope_label: The meal and drink offerings, and one law for the stranger

schools.summary: Gill identifies the audience narrowly: those of twenty years old and upward had been sworn to die in the wilderness, so the people Moses is told to address are the younger sort, who should actually possess the land. He notes that the wine had to be wine of the grapes, on the Targum's authority, no other sort being permissible; and on the stranger he agrees with Calvin that the proselyte of righteousness is meant, not the stranger of the gate. Calvin reads the single form of worship as a guard for uniformity, and gives two reasons for it: that proselytes lately incorporated might devote themselves the more cheerfully to piety when they saw themselves placed in the same position as the children of Abraham, and that if any distinction were made, corrupt mixtures would immediately creep in — so that lest the purity of God's worship should be gradually corrupted by absurd imitation, the gate was shut against the variety which usually draws men aside in different directions.

Clarke reports the opinion of some learned men that several offerings prescribed by the law were never intended to be made in the wilderness at all, which did not afford the conveniences the worship required, but only in the promised land. On the one law for the stranger he draws a conclusion opposite to Calvin's: one form of worship was a necessity in that land, surrounded as it was by idolatrous nations, and it was right that those who conformed should have equal rights and privileges, as indeed they did; but under the Christian dispensation no particular form is prescribed and the types are fulfilled, so unlimited toleration should be allowed, and while the sacred writings are made the basis of the worship offered to God, every man should be permitted to worship according to his own conscience. Wesley hears a promise inside the preamble — I give you means I will certainly give you, notwithstanding this great provocation — and states the principle behind the tables of quantities in a sentence: two tenth deals for the ram because it belonged to a better sacrifice than the lamb, and three for the bullock, so that the accessory sacrifice grows proportionably with the principal. He converts the measures as well, a tenth deal being the tenth part of an ephah, about five pints, and a hin about five quarts; and he limits the equality granted to the stranger to religion rather than civil standing, a presage of the future calling of the Gentiles, but no warrant for partaking of Israel's civil privileges.

Ellicott places the rule among its neighbours: the meal and drink offerings ordered here for a lamb are the same as those appointed to accompany the morning and evening lamb, and offerings of this kind had already been prescribed in connection with the three great feasts. He prefers a special vow to the received rendering at the eighth verse, and gives the literal sense of the clause about the congregation, noting that some render it as a vocative instead. Keil draws the arithmetic out, the number of appointed quantities being required to correspond to the number of sacrificial animals, and pauses over a grammatical oddity, a third-person verb standing between two second-person forms, which he calls certainly striking and unusual, but not so offensive as to make it necessary to alter the text.

debates.question: What follows from there being one law for Israelite and stranger?

positions.position: uniformity — one prescribed form, lest variety and corrupt mixtures creep into the worship of God
under the gospel, toleration — no particular form being prescribed, every man should worship according to his own conscience
religious equality only, and a presage of the calling of the Gentiles; strangers were not thereby given Israel's civil privileges

outliers.note: turns a ceremonial equality into an argument for religious liberty under the gospel, which is the reverse of the use Calvin makes of the same verse

themes: the accessory that grows with the principal
one law for the home-born and the stranger
uniformity of worship, and what follows from it

17.pericope_label: The heave offering of the first of the dough

schools.summary: Gill supplies almost everything the passage does not say. The law binds Israelites only, so that the dough of a Gentile is free from the cake even though an Israelite kneads it; by bread is meant bread corn, and specifically the old corn of the land which they first ate on entering it, the Targum excluding rice and millet and pulse, and the Jewish authorities naming five grains only from which the cake was required. The obligation covers dough made for men's bread and no other. On the quantity he observes that the text does not express it at all, leaving it to the people's generosity with no stinted measure fixed by law; tradition rather than statute supplies the figure, the elders making it the twenty-fourth part of the first dough kneaded — not the forty-fourth, as Buxtorf through mistake says — with the Targum agreeing at one part in twenty-four and the Mishnah lowering the share to a forty-eighth for dough made to be sold publicly. He records one further attempt at the number resting on the spelling, since the word begins and ends with the letter standing numerically for forty, which some have taken as an instruction to the bountiful man to give a fortieth. He reads the heaving itself as an acknowledgment that God is the sovereign Lord and possessor of heaven and earth and the owner and proprietor of the land of Canaan. Calvin asks why the offering is made of dough rather than grain, and answers best of any: first-fruits were already offered of their fruits and their ears of corn, but the representation was more lively in the bread itself, so God would have them present tokens of their gratitude not only from the barn but from the mill and the oven, that while they were eating their bread also they might have him before their eyes.
Wesley fixes the timing, that the offering falls not after the eating but before it, when they are about to eat, and glosses the bread of the land as bread corn.
Ellicott confines himself to the word, which may be rendered mixed meal, is used only in the plural, and outside these two verses occurs only twice in the whole Old Testament.

outliers.note: shows the whole weight of the rule resting on tradition rather than text — the law names no quantity, and the twenty-fourth part, the forty-eighth, and the fortieth all come from elsewhere

themes: first-fruits from the oven, not only the barn
a quantity the law leaves unfixed
who is bound by the law of the cake

22.pericope_label: Sins of ignorance, and the offerings that cover them

schools.summary: Gill widens the word before anything else: every sin is an error, a missing of the mark, a wandering from the way of God's commandments; and though Jarchi and the Jewish writers generally take the passage of idolatry, it rather respects any deviation from the law, moral or ceremonial, and especially the latter. Calvin sharpens it toward something more culpable than accident, since the word extends to incogitancy, which partakes of contempt of God and arises from too great security, when men inconsiderately fall into the sins their lusts invite them to — which is why deliberate impiety is set against it afterwards. He finds no new law here at all, only a relaxation of an old one: two bullocks were commanded before, one for a burnt offering and one for a sin offering, and permission is given here to substitute a goat if the second were not easily obtained, so that Leviticus delivers the regular and perfect rite while this passage adds the permissive alteration. And he states what the whole provision is for — since nothing is easier than for men to err, the remedy was most necessary lest those who had sinned should fall into despair, so that when the people or private persons saw their guilt, and might have despaired of pardon and thrown away the pursuit of holiness, God anticipates them and shews by what means he is to be propitiated, that the sins which had occurred should not interrupt his service.

Henry keeps both halves of the balance. Sins committed ignorantly still need atoning for, since ignorance will in a degree excuse but will not justify those who might have known their Lord's will and did it not, which is why David prayed to be cleansed from his secret faults, the errors he did not himself understand. And they are forgiven, through the great sacrifice, who when he offered himself once for all upon the cross seemed to explain the intention of that offering in the prayer, Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do; Paul alludes to this same law when he says he obtained mercy because he did it ignorantly and in unbelief. Henry reads the congregational case as a national sin become customary through a vulgar error — the ceremonial observances being so numerous that some might by degrees be forgotten, as particularly the heave offering of the dough just prescribed — and notes what looked favourably on the Gentiles, that this atonement for ignorance is expressly extended to those who were strangers to the commonwealth of Israel.

Wesley distinguishes this law from the earlier one by the kind of fault it covers: the Leviticus statute speaks of a positive miscarriage, of doing about the holy things of God what ought not to have been done, whereas this speaks only of an omission of something that ought to have been done about holy ceremonies. Clarke divides the material differently, taking the case here to refer to the whole congregation and the cases just before to the sin of an individual, and observes that even sins committed through ignorance required an atonement, which God in his mercy has provided.

Ellicott fixes the technical sense, that shegagah denotes transgressions committed unwittingly, standing in contrast to the sin done presumptuously later in the chapter, and reaches Wesley's distinction from the other side: provision had been made for sins of commission unwittingly committed by the whole congregation, but none appears to have been made for the guilt contracted by sins of omission. He adds two supports — the offerings differ, a young bullock being the sin offering there while here the bullock is a burnt offering and a kid the sin offering, and the commandments of this chapter have express reference to the land of Canaan, whereas many delivered earlier were already binding — and notes that the individual case here carries no restriction to sins of commission. Keil confirms the reach of the law, that the rule laid down for Israelites is here raised into general validity for foreigners as well.

debates.question: Why repeat a law for sins of ignorance that Leviticus has already given?

positions.position: the earlier law covered doing what ought not to be done; this covers omitting what ought to be done
the earlier cases were of individuals, this of the whole congregation
it is not a new law but a relaxation of the old — permission to substitute a goat where the second bullock could not easily be had

outliers.note: reads the congregational case as a ceremony quietly forgotten over generations rather than a sin committed, and points to the dough offering of the preceding paragraph as exactly the kind of thing that would lapse

themes: error, incogitancy, and what ignorance excuses
omission against commission
a remedy given lest the sinner despair

30.pericope_label: The soul that doeth ought with a high hand

schools.summary: Gill fills in the manner from the Targum's through pride — haughty, insolent, bold and daring, obstinate and self-willed, done with purpose and design, openly and publicly, neither fearing God nor regarding man — and marks what the reason clause does not mean, since the presumptuous man has broken the commandment through contempt of it, despising it as a command of God, whereas those who sin ignorantly break it too. Calvin agrees about the posture and then narrows the offence sharply. To deal with a high hand is nothing more than to attempt or undertake proudly what is not lawful, since our hands ought to be guided and as it were restrained by God's word; but although men's hands are used in many acts of audacity, what is meant here in particular is the profanation of God's true and legitimate worship, when anything is invented inconsistent with its purity, for the punishment is not decreed against thefts or murders or other such crimes, but against the perverse imaginations which tend to the corruption of religion. All self-invented services betray an impious contempt of God, as if men designedly despised him and spurned at his commands, whence he infers that nothing is more opposed to perfect and sincere religion than the temerity which induces men to follow whatever course they please. The closing clause he allows two senses, either confirming the justice of the punishment or warning that the impiety should be corrected betimes, before it has advanced too far.

Henry defines the sin by intent rather than by degree. Presumptuous sinners are those who avowedly confront God's authority and set up their own lust in competition with it, who sin for sinning's sake in contradiction to the precept and in defiance of the penalty, who fight against God and dare him to do his worst; it is not only to sin against knowledge but to sin designedly against God's will and glory. He then puts the speech into the sinner's mouth: the language of presumptuous sin is that eternal truth is not fit to be believed, the Lord of all not fit to be obeyed, and almighty power not fit to be either feared or trusted, so that it imputes folly to Infinite Wisdom and iniquity to the righteous Judge of heaven and earth. Many come short of fulfilling the word and yet value it and count the law honourable; the presumptuous despise it, thinking themselves too great and too good and too wise to be ruled by it — and whatever the sin itself is, it is the contumacy that incurs the anathema. There remains no sacrifice for such sins, since the law provided none; and Henry passes on the Jewish doctors' reading of the last clause, that the iniquity cleaves to the soul after it is cut off, to be accounted for at the great day.

Clarke states the ground of the sentence: bold daring acts of transgression against the fullest evidence and in despite of the divine authority admitted of no atonement, and the presumption probably implied an utter contempt of the word and authority of God springing from an idolatrous or atheistical mind, in which case all repentance was precluded by the very denial of God's word and being. Wesley reduces the offence to the insult it contains — the man sets God at defiance and exposes him to contempt, as if he were unable to punish transgressors.
Ellicott gives the phrase literally, with a high hand, and corrects the verb that follows, which is not reproacheth but blasphemeth.

debates.question: What kind of sin does 'with a high hand' cover?

positions.position: any sin done in open defiance of God's authority, in contradiction to the precept and in defiance of the penalty
specifically the corruption of God's worship by invention — the penalty is not decreed against thefts or murders but against perverse imaginations in religion

outliers.note: restricts the death penalty of this verse to offences against worship, explicitly excluding theft and murder from its scope — a narrower reading than any of the others give it

themes: sinning with a high hand
contumacy rather than the act
a sin the law provides no sacrifice for

32.pericope_label: The man who gathered sticks on the sabbath

schools.summary: Gill reports the common Jewish view, from Aben Ezra, that though the incident is recorded here it belongs to the first year, soon after the sabbath law was given, which produces Jarchi's remark that Scripture tells it to Israel's reproach, since they kept only the first sabbath and on the second this man came and profaned it. Gill himself puts it later, in the wilderness of Paran, after the spies and the discomfiture, where it stands in its proper place as an instance of the presumptuous sinner just described. He adds from the Targum that the man was admonished first and would not desist, places the ward in a certain prison in the camp — perhaps the very one in which the blasphemer had been kept, and for much the same reason — and notes that Moses consulted the Lord in the tabernacle, from above the mercy seat, where he had promised to meet him. Calvin declines to date the episode, since we know neither the year nor the month, and reflects on it in two directions at once. The Israelites were not always affected by the same degree of madness, and here their moderation is as manifest as the fervency of their zeal: they bring the transgressor to authority rather than dealing with him themselves, they quietly wait for the decision of God, and they execute the sentence promptly once it is given. Yet since the most trifling occasion led them astray soon afterwards, their hypocrisy was betrayed by that levity — one swallow does not make a spring, and we judge a whole life wrongly from a single noble action. It may well be that the men who brought him were careless in other matters and, as hypocrites usually are, excessively rigid about an outward ceremony. From the punishment Calvin infers that the offender had not erred through inadvertence but in gross contempt, since God would not have commanded stoning otherwise; and he draws two conclusions, that the sabbath was the mark by which God separated his people from the heathen, though its object was never mere idleness but that they should renounce their own works and live to God, and that the magistrate is appointed to maintain the first table no less than the second, since the man was not stoned by an unreflecting impulse but by the direct command of God, no political law having yet been given on the point.

Clarke reads the case as an illustration of the verses before it — the man despised the word of the Lord and therefore broke his commandment, and on that ground was punished with the utmost rigour of the law. Wesley agrees that the law of the sabbath was plain and positive, so that this transgression must needs be a known and wilful sin, and clears up two details of the procedure: those who brought him brought him to the rulers of the congregation, and what was uncertain was not the crime but the manner in which he should be cut off, since it was known in general that sabbath-breakers were to be put to death.

Ellicott prefers to begin the sentence afresh — now the children of Israel were in the wilderness, and they found — and takes the incident to be recorded in order to illustrate the presumptuous sins just made capital. All that is certain is that it happened in the wilderness, according to Ibn Ezra at Sinai but more probably during the wanderings after Kadesh, and no inference can be drawn from the verse about when the account was written down. He confirms Wesley's reading of the difficulty from the wording: death had already been denounced against those who profaned the day, but the manner of inflicting it does not appear to have been declared before, and the very verb used here recurs in the parallel case of the blasphemer, whom they also put in ward that the mind of the Lord might be shewed them. Keil reads the placement itself as the argument, the history being inserted as a practical illustration of sinning with a high hand, and takes the congregation before whom the man was brought to be the college of elders acting as the judicial authority.

positions.position: in the first year, soon after the sabbath law was given — on the second sabbath Israel ever kept
later, during the wanderings after Kadesh, where the narrative places it as an instance of presumptuous sin
unknowable; nothing is better than to follow the order Moses gives

outliers.note: praises the people's conduct here in every particular and then withdraws the praise, on the ground that men who lapse at the next trifle were being rigid about an outward ceremony rather than obedient

themes: when and where the episode belongs
the crime known, the sentence not
zeal that does not prove the heart

37.pericope_label: The tassels on the corners of the garment

schools.summary: Gill sets out who was bound — Israelites, priests, Levites, proselytes and freed servants, but not Gentiles, who might not make them at all — and passes on Jarchi's judgment that this precept is equivalent to all the commandments, which he makes the reason for its being placed here. Calvin guards the institution from both sides. There was no religion in the fringes themselves and no value in the material texture, but since men are lazy and forgetful in the cultivation of piety, God made provision for their infirmity; in telling them to look upon it and remember, he hints that they need coarse rudiments which strike the outward senses, nothing being likelier than that forgetfulness should steal upon them. Yet God has no satisfaction in empty knowledge, and demands serious affections and practical performance. On the prohibition Calvin presses hardest of any: by contrasting men's hearts and eyes with his Law, God shews that he would have his people contented with the one rule he prescribes, without the admixture of their own imaginations, and denounces the vanity of whatever men invent for themselves, however pleasing. The last word of the verse makes it plain, that men go a whoring whenever they are governed by their own counsels — for those who worship God by their own will account their zeal very good, and do nothing but pollute themselves with spiritual adultery, since what the world considers the holiest devotion, God with his own mouth pronounces to be fornication.

Henry reads the law as the counterpart of the one before it: provision had just been made for the pardon of sins of ignorance, and here is an expedient for preventing them, a memorandum against sinning through forgetfulness. He notes that the Jews were distinguished from their neighbours in dress as in diet, taught by such little instances of singularity not to be conformed to the way of the heathen in greater things, and that they proclaimed themselves Jews wherever they went, as not ashamed of God and his law. The tassels were not appointed for the trimming and adorning of clothes but to stir up their pure minds by way of remembrance — many look upon their ornaments to feed their pride, but these were to awaken the conscience. He insists that the phylacteries were a different thing altogether, of the Pharisees' own invention, whereas the fringes were a divine institution, and records that the Jews wear them still, saying as they put them on, blessed be he who has sanctified us unto himself and commanded us to wear fringes. The prohibition he takes as a preservative from idolatry in particular, though extending to the whole conversation, since nothing is more contrary to God's honour and our own interest than to walk in the way of our heart and the sight of our eyes.

Clarke asks how a tassel can carry a commandment and answers with an argument about signs. It would be bold to assert any analogy between a fringe and a precept; but when one thing is appointed to represent another, however unlike, the first becomes the regular sign of the second. There is no analogy between the word bread and the substance it stands for, yet because the word represents the thing, everyone understands it, and the sight of it conveys not its letters but the thing signified; so with the tassels, appointed by God to bring the commandments to mind, they conveyed the intelligence intended. Wesley describes the object itself, threads standing out further than the rest at the four borders of the upper garment, with the riband added to make it more obvious to the sight, its colour blue or purple; and he gives the two forbidden errors names — enquire not for other ways of serving me than I have prescribed, neither after the devices of your own hearts, as Nadab and Abihu did when they offered strange fire, nor after the examples your eyes see, as you did when you worshipped a calf after the manner of Egypt.

Ellicott corrects the picture: these are tassels rather than fringes, set on the corners of the garment, and the garment itself was a four-cornered cloth which the poor also used as a counterpane, commonly worn with a hole in the centre for the head. The Pharisees enlarged them to exhibit their punctilious fulfilment of the Law, and great sanctity was attached to them, which is why the woman with the issue of blood desired to touch one of our Saviour's. Keil supplies the occasion, taking the command to have been prompted by the incident just recorded, and reads the tassel with its dark blue thread as a memorial sign, that seeing it the Israelites might remember the commandments and not stray after their own hearts and eyes.

outliers.note: defends the arbitrariness of the sign as the ordinary condition of all signs, arguing from the word 'bread' that representation needs no resemblance to work

themes: a sign appointed to carry a commandment
preventing the sins the last law pardoned
seeking after one’s own heart and eyes
